title: The Power of Strategic Subtraction
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Admired Leadership argues that leaders handle new priorities badly because they default to adding work and almost never consider removing any. The piece cites research showing the bias toward addition grows stronger when people are busy, so new priorities simply stack on top of old ones and the team pays in longer hours and thinner attention. The proposed fix is to make every addition a trade, so that something must come off the list before a new priority goes on. Because conscientious people will keep doing old work out of loyalty, leaders must name explicitly what is being stopped or postponed and why. Subtraction works best as a calendared habit, using Peter Drucker's question about whether you would start the work today, and by asking the people closest to the work what can go. The closing point is that the best leaders are as skilled at taking priorities away as at adding them.
points: People under pressure default to adding rather than removing, so a leader has to counter that bias on purpose.
Make every new priority a trade: nothing goes on the list until something else comes off it.
Loyal, conscientious staff will not stop old work without explicit permission, so name what is being dropped and why.
Schedule a regular priority review and apply Drucker's test: if we did not already do this, would we start it now?
Ask the people closest to the work what must stay and what can go, since they usually already know.
quotes: Choosing to stop doing valuable but lower-priority work is among the most important decisions leaders make. Leaders who actively decide what tasks, processes, and initiatives to scrap understand the critical importance of strategic subtraction for creating team effectiveness.
Research confirms that when people try to improve something, they default to adding new elements and overlook the option of removing existing ones. The bias grows stronger when people are busy.
The team pays for that choice in longer hours, thinner attention, and slower progress on all fronts.
Leaders must recognize that conscientious people will keep doing old work out of loyalty unless they are given explicit permission to stop.

Deciding what not to do starts with Peter Drucker’s question: “If we did not already do this, would we go into it now?” Good leaders are mindful of work kept alive because of sunk costs or by a senior leader’s attachment.
Good leaders make a point of asking the people closest to the work for their view. They usually know exactly what must stay and what can go.
Every leader knows how to add new priorities. The best ones understand it is just as important to take some away.
